script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Good afternoon, Harbour Car Hire. What can I do for you?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: I'd like to hire a car for a long weekend, from Friday the twelfth to Monday the fifteenth.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Would you prefer an automatic or a manual?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Automatic please. And a small car, something economical.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: We have the Fiesta and the Corsa. The Corsa is slightly bigger and costs thirty-eight pounds a day, while the Fiesta is thirty-two.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: I'll take the Fiesta then.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Good. Basic insurance is included, but full cover costs an extra eight pounds a day.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: I'll take the full cover, to be safe.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Will you be driving outside the country?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: No, only within the region.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Pick-up is from our airport branch. Please bring your driving licence and a credit card in your name.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Is there a late return fee?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Yes, returns after six in the evening cost an extra thirty pounds.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Okay. My reference is HC four four one.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Thank you. Enjoy your trip.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Do you have child seats available?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Yes, we can supply child seats for an extra charge of five pounds a day. Please tell us the age of the child when you book.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Okay, I'll think about that.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Of course. Also, the car must be returned with a full tank of fuel, otherwise we charge for refuelling at a higher rate.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Understood. Is there a mileage limit?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: No, the mileage is unlimited for this booking.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Great. How do I collect the keys?

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Go to the desk in the arrivals hall. Show your confirmation email and the staff will hand you the keys and documents.

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: Perfect. Thanks for your help.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Is there anything else I can help you with today?

script.speaker: Customer
script.text: No, that's everything.

script.speaker: Agent
script.text: Have a safe journey.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Welcome to the Old Mill Quarter walk. This tour takes about ninety minutes and starts outside the town hall.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The mill was built in eighteen twenty-two and produced flour until the nineteen-thirties. Its wheel is still original.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Next we go down to the canal. Barges carried coal along it from the mines, and the towpath is now a popular cycle route.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The brick warehouse on your left was used to store cloth. It has been converted into apartments, but the external walls are protected, so no alterations to them are allowed.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Our final stop is St Anne's church. The bell tower was added in eighteen eighty and is the tallest structure in the quarter.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Please remember that the church asks for a donation of two pounds to enter the crypt. Photography is allowed everywhere except inside the crypt.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Toilets are available at the café by the canal, which opens at ten.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Before we leave the mill, notice the millstones on the ground floor. They were cut from a single block of granite and are much heavier than they look.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The old granary next to the mill has been turned into a small exhibition. It shows photographs of the workers and the tools they used, and the displays are free to visit.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Walking east along the canal, you'll pass a row of cottages that were once home to the boatmen's families. Their gardens are still well kept, and some residents are happy to talk to visitors if you ask politely.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: The towpath can be muddy after rain, so wear sensible shoes. There is a bench halfway along, and it makes an ideal spot for a short break.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: If you have children with you, the playground near the church is a good place for them to run around while you finish the tour.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Thank you for joining the walk today. The tour map, with all the stops marked, is available from the town hall and from the café.

script.speaker: Guide
script.text: Please note that the town hall displays are closed on public holidays, so plan your visit accordingly.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Have you read the methods for our memory experiment yet?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Yes. Participants memorise a list of twenty words, then recall them after a delay.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: The delay is the important part. The professor wants us to test three intervals: immediate, five minutes, and twenty-four hours.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: So three groups? Or does each person do all three?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Each person does all three, in a counterbalanced order, so that practice doesn't bias the results.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Good. How many participants do we need?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: The minimum is forty, and the ethics committee has approved up to sixty.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Forty sounds tight if people drop out.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Yes, which is why we'll recruit from two departments, not just ours.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: What about the word list? Do we make our own?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: No, we use the standard list from the lab. It's been checked for word frequency already.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: And the analysis? Is it SPSS?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: The professor prefers R, so we'll learn that over the holiday.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: I'll need a tutorial for that.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: I'll send you one. Our report is due on the ninth of February.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Who's going to be the research assistant on the testing days?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Priya offered. She's done the procedure before, so she can run the sessions and keep the timing accurate.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: That's good. What about the consent forms?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: They're being translated into two other languages, because some participants won't be comfortable in English.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Smart. And we need a debrief at the end, right?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Yes, we'll explain the purpose after each session and answer any questions. That's required by the committee.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Fine. I'll draft the debrief script tonight.

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Great. Let's meet on Thursday to review the timing schedule together.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Do we need ethics approval for the consent forms as well?

script.speaker: Maya
script.text: Yes, the committee has to approve the final versions before testing begins.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: In this lecture we'll examine the urban heat island effect, the way cities become warmer than the surrounding rural areas.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The difference is often several degrees at night. Dark roofs and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: A major cause is the loss of vegetation. Trees and grass cool the air through evaporation, so cities with fewer green spaces tend to be hotter.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Tall buildings also play a role. They trap heat between them and reduce the air flow that would otherwise carry it away.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The health effects are serious. Heat waves in cities are linked to more hospital admissions, particularly among older adults.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Planners have several responses. Green roofs, tree-lined streets and light-coloured paving can reduce temperatures significantly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Some cities have also introduced cooling centres, which open during heat alerts.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: One common misconception is that the effect is only a problem in very large cities. In fact, even towns of a few tens of thousands of people show measurable heat islands.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Let's look at how the effect is measured. Researchers use weather stations in the city centre and in rural areas nearby, then compare temperatures at the same time of day.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Satellite data is also useful, because it can show surface temperatures across a whole region. However, surface readings are not the same as air temperatures, so both methods are needed.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The effect varies with the seasons. It is generally strongest during calm, clear summer nights, when there is little wind to mix the air and the ground cannot cool quickly.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Cities can adapt in simple ways. Painting roofs white, planting street trees with wide canopies, and designing parks that connect to residential areas all help to reduce the build-up of heat.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Community involvement matters too. Residents who know which streets become hottest can help councils decide where to place shade structures and water fountains.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: Next week we'll consider the economic costs of heat, including energy demand for air conditioning and lost productivity in workplaces during heat waves. Please read the case study on a large coastal city in the course pack before the seminar, and be ready to discuss how its planning rules have changed. Remember that the mid-term essay is due in three weeks.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: The seminar will also cover ways that architects can reduce heat in new buildings. Students who attended last year's session found the case studies especially useful for their assignments.
